ox: Wrong. This uses the overall stoichiometry (two B consumed). Rate laws for multistep reactions come from the slow step. The trap is reading the exponent from the overall equation.
Wrong. C is an intermediate, made in step 1 and used up in step 2. It cannot be in the final rate law, and step 2 is fast. The trap is using the fast step.
Wrong. D is the final product. Products generally do not appear in the initial rate law. The trap is thinking more product speeds the rate.
Correct. The slow step A + B -> C controls the speed. Its reactants A and B are each first order, so rate = k[A][B].

p: Many reactions happen in several steps called a mechanism. The slowest step limits the overall speed, like the narrowest part of a road. It is called the rate-determining step.
The rate law uses the reactants of that slow step, with exponents equal to their coefficients in that step. Intermediates are not allowed in the final rate law.

d_5E_12.eli: A line of kids at a water fountain moves at the speed of the slowest drinker. The rest do not matter.
mem: Rate law comes from the slow step, not the overall equation.
Elementary-step coefficients equal the exponents.
Intermediates must not appear in the final rate law.
d_5E_12.trap: Do not write the rate law from overall stoichiometry. Use the slow step.
d_5E_12.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. If the surroundings cool, the reaction absorbed heat, which is endothermic and gives a positive ΔH. This option mixes endothermic cooling with a negative ΔH.
Wrong. The temperature rise is right, but exothermic means ΔH is negative. The trap is a sign error.
Correct. An exothermic reaction releases heat. The surroundings (the calorimeter contents) warm up, and ΔH is negative because the system lost energy.
Wrong. Energy is conserved but it moves from the system to the surroundings as heat. The calorimeter temperature changes. The trap is misusing conservation of energy.

p: The system is the reaction itself. The surroundings are everything else, such as the water in a calorimeter. Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat the system gives or takes at constant pressure.
Exothermic: the system releases heat, so ΔH is negative and the surroundings get warmer. Endothermic: the system absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive and the surroundings get colder.

d_5E_15.eli: A campfire gives off heat. The fire loses energy, but the people around it get warm.
mem: Exothermic: ΔH < 0, surroundings warm.
Endothermic: ΔH > 0, surroundings cool.
ΔH is from the system's point of view.
d_5E_15.trap: Watch the viewpoint. Heat leaving the system warms the surroundings.
d_5E_15.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. The transition state is the peak of the energy curve. It exists for an instant and cannot be isolated.
Wrong. A valley between two peaks is a reaction intermediate. Intermediates can sometimes be isolated. The trap is mixing up peaks and valleys.
Wrong. The energy of the products is the final level of the diagram. It is not a peak. The trap is thinking the end point is the transition state.
Wrong. The difference between reactant and product energies is ΔG or ΔH, which is a number, not a species. The trap is confusing a difference with a point on the curve.

p: A reaction coordinate diagram plots energy as a reaction goes from reactants to products. The highest point on the curve is the transition state, a fleeting arrangement of atoms in mid-change. The height from reactants to this peak is the activation energy.
A valley between two peaks is an intermediate. It is a real species with some stability, so it can sometimes be detected or isolated.

d_5E_17.eli: Rolling a ball over a hill: the very top is the transition state, but the ball cannot stay there. A flat dip on the way is a resting spot, the intermediate.
mem: Transition state = peak, cannot be isolated.
Intermediate = valley, may be isolated.
Activation energy = reactants to the peak.
d_5E_17.trap: Peak is transition state; valley is intermediate. Do not swap them.
d_5E_17.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. All-temperature spontaneity needs negative ΔH and positive ΔS. Here ΔS is negative, so -TΔS becomes a positive term that grows with T.
Wrong. High-temperature-only spontaneity needs positive ΔH and positive ΔS. Students flip the signs and pick this.
Wrong. Never spontaneous needs positive ΔH and negative ΔS. Here ΔH is negative, which helps at low T.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. With both negative, ΔH is a negative (helpful) term. At low T the -TΔS term is small, so ΔG stays negative. At high T, -TΔS becomes a big positive number and wins.

concept.t: Sign of ΔG depends on ΔH, ΔS and T
p: ΔG tells us if a reaction is spontaneous (happens on its own). ΔG below zero means spontaneous. The equation is ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. ΔH is heat change, ΔS is disorder change, and T is temperature in kelvin.
If ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, temperature decides the winner. Both negative: ΔH wins at low T, so it is spontaneous when cold.

d_5E_20.eli: Think of a snowman: it forms (stays together) when it is cold, but it falls apart when it is hot. Order is allowed only when the temperature is low.
mem: ΔH negative, ΔS positive: always spontaneous
ΔH positive, ΔS negative: never spontaneous
Both negative: spontaneous at LOW T
Both positive: spontaneous at HIGH T
d_5E_20.sc: When signs match, ask which term wins. Low T shrinks the TΔS term, so ΔH wins. High T makes TΔS win.
d_5E_20.trap: Mixing up which same-sign combination goes with low T and which goes with high T.
d_5E_20.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Positive ΔG would mean Q is greater than K and the reaction would run in reverse. Here Q is less than K.
Wrong. Negative ΔG means forward direction, so the two parts of this option contradict each other.
Correct. ΔG = RT ln(Q/K). If Q is less than K, then Q/K is below 1 and its natural log is negative, so ΔG is negative. The reaction goes forward, making products until Q rises to equal K.
Wrong. ΔG is zero only at equilibrium, where Q = K. Here Q is less than K, so it is not at equilibrium.

p: Q is the reaction quotient: the ratio of products to reactants right now. K is the same ratio at equilibrium. Comparing them tells you which way the reaction must move.
Q less than K means too few products. The reaction goes forward (makes products). Q greater than K means too many products, so it goes in reverse.

d_5E_3.eli: If a pot has less soup than the recipe wants, you keep cooking forward until it reaches the right amount.
mem: Q < K: forward, ΔG negative
Q > K: reverse, ΔG positive
Q = K: equilibrium, ΔG = 0
ΔG = RT ln(Q/K)

fm.f: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K), where R = gas constant, T = temperature in kelvin, Q = reaction quotient, K = equilibrium constant
fm.s: ln of a number below 1 is negative, so ΔG = RT x (negative) = negative
fm.why: It links the current mixture to the direction of change.
fm.nc: You only need the sign of ln, not a number: below 1 is negative, above 1 is positive.

d_5E_3.sc: Q small means few products, so the reaction goes right (forward).
d_5E_3.trap: Reversing the Q/K comparison. Q less than K means too many reactants, so the shift is forward.
d_5E_3.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Breaking bonds takes energy (endothermic). Forming bonds gives energy off (exothermic). So ΔH is roughly energy of bonds broken minus energy of bonds formed.
Wrong. Breaking a bond always costs energy. The trap is the idea that 'breaking' releases energy, like ATP hydrolysis folklore. Really the energy comes from forming new, stronger bonds.
Wrong. Forming a bond releases energy because the atoms move to a lower energy state.
Wrong. Breaking is endothermic, so both cannot be exothermic.

p: Bond energy is the energy needed to pull two bonded atoms apart. Since you must put energy in, breaking is endothermic (absorbs heat). When atoms join, the same amount comes back out, so forming is exothermic (releases heat).
ΔH is the heat change of a reaction. ΔH = energy in to break old bonds minus energy out from forming new bonds.

d_5E_9.eli: Pulling two magnets apart takes effort. When they snap together, they give back a click of energy.
mem: Break bonds: energy IN (endothermic)
Form bonds: energy OUT (exothermic)
ΔH ≈ Σ broken - Σ formed
Stronger bonds formed than broken means ΔH negative
d_5E_9.trap: Thinking energy is released when a bond breaks.
d_5E_9.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. A catalyst gives the reaction an easier path with a lower activation energy (the energy hill to start). It speeds forward and reverse equally, so ΔG and K do not change.
Wrong. A catalyst only gets you to equilibrium faster. It does not change where equilibrium sits, because K is unchanged.
Wrong. ΔG depends only on the start and end states (state function). A catalyst changes the path, not the endpoints.
Wrong. A catalyst is regenerated at the end of each cycle, so it is not used up. Students confuse it with a reactant.

p: A catalyst is a helper that makes a reaction faster by lowering activation energy, the energy hill reactants must climb. It does this by offering a different route.
The start and end energies stay the same, so ΔG, ΔH and K do not change. The catalyst is not used up. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

q84.eli: A catalyst is a tunnel through a hill. You get to the other side faster, but the other side is still the same place.
mem: Lowers Ea, speeds both directions equally
Does not change ΔG, ΔH or K
Not consumed
Does not shift equilibrium
q84.trap: Thinking a catalyst makes a reaction more favorable (more negative ΔG) or shifts it toward products.
q84.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. With ΔH negative, and ΔS positive making -TΔS also negative, both terms are negative at any T. So ΔG is always negative.
Wrong. High T only is for ΔH positive and ΔS positive.
Wrong. Low T only is for ΔH negative and ΔS negative.
Wrong. Never spontaneous is ΔH positive and ΔS negative.

p: A reaction is spontaneous (goes on its own) if ΔG is negative. ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, where T is temperature in kelvin (always positive).
Negative ΔH means heat is released, which is favorable. Positive ΔS means more disorder, which is also favorable. Both help, so ΔG is negative at every temperature.

q85.eli: A ball rolling downhill that is also being pushed from behind will always roll.
mem: -ΔH, +ΔS: always spontaneous
+ΔH, -ΔS: never spontaneous
Same signs: temperature decides
q85.trap: Mixing up the four sign combinations.
q85.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Halving the volume raises pressure. Le Chatelier's principle says the system relieves the stress by moving to the side with fewer gas moles. Left has 1 + 3 = 4 moles, right has 2 moles, so it shifts toward NH₃.
Wrong. The N₂ and H₂ side has more gas moles (4), so it would raise pressure further. This is the reverse of the correct shift.
Wrong. No shift happens only when both sides have equal gas moles. Here it is 4 versus 2.
Wrong. K changes only with temperature. Pressure or volume changes shift the position but not the value of K.

p: Le Chatelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts to partly undo the disturbance. Squeezing a gas mixture raises pressure.
The system lowers pressure by making fewer gas molecules. Count gas moles on each side and move toward the smaller number. K itself does not change.

q86.eli: In a crowded room, if the room shrinks, people pair up to take less space.
mem: Volume down or pressure up: shift to fewer gas moles
Volume up: shift to more gas moles
Equal moles: no shift
Only temperature changes K
q86.sc: Count the gas coefficients on each side. Squeeze goes toward the smaller number.
q86.trap: Thinking K changes when pressure or volume changes.
q86.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. First order means doubling [A] doubles the rate (2¹ = 2), not quadruples it.
Correct. Rate is proportional to [A]ⁿ. Doubling [A] multiplies rate by 2ⁿ. The rate rose 4 times, and 2² = 4, so n = 2.
Wrong. Zero order means rate does not depend on [A] (2⁰ = 1), so the rate would not change.
Wrong. Fourth order would give 2⁴ = 16 times the rate. The students confuse the factor 4 with the order.

p: Reaction order tells how rate depends on a concentration. In rate = k[A]ⁿ, n is the order, and k is the rate constant.
If you change [A] by a factor and the rate changes by another factor, then (concentration factor)ⁿ = (rate factor). Solve for n.

q87.eli: If doubling your pizza order makes the mess four times bigger, the mess grows by the square.
mem: Double [A], rate x1: zero order
Double [A], rate x2: first order
Double [A], rate x4: second order

fm.f: (factor in [A])ⁿ = (factor in rate), where n = order in A
fm.why: Rate follows [A]ⁿ, so scaling [A] scales rate by that power.
fm.nc: Ask: 2 to what power gives 4? Answer: 2.

q87.trap: Picking 'fourth' because the rate changed by 4.
q87.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. In an endothermic reaction, heat is like a reactant. Adding heat (raising T) pushes the reaction toward products, so K increases.
Wrong. K decreases with higher T for exothermic reactions, where heat is a product. The trap is mixing up the two.
Wrong. K depends on temperature. It is the only common thing that changes K.
Wrong. Higher T speeds the rate, but it also changes K. 'Only rate' is wrong.

p: K is the equilibrium constant: the ratio of products to reactants when things stop changing. Temperature is the one thing that changes K.

Treat heat as a reactant or product. Endothermic (absorbs heat): heat is a reactant, so adding heat favors products and K goes up. Exothermic: heat is a product, so adding heat favors reactants and K goes down.

q88.eli: If a recipe needs heat to work, a hotter oven makes more of the finished dish.
mem: Endothermic: T up, K up
Exothermic: T up, K down
Only T changes K
q88.sc: Write 'heat' on the reactant or product side, then apply Le Chatelier.
q88.trap: Applying the exothermic rule to an endothermic reaction.
q88.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. A closed system lets energy (heat and work) cross its boundary but not matter. A sealed flask you can heat is an example.
Wrong. An open system exchanges both matter and energy, like an open pot of boiling water.
Wrong. An isolated system exchanges neither. A perfect thermos is the idea.
Wrong. Isothermal means constant temperature. It describes a process, not what crosses the boundary.

p: The system is the part of the universe we study. The surroundings are everything else. We classify systems by what can cross the boundary between them.
Open: matter and energy cross. Closed: only energy crosses. Isolated: nothing crosses.

x5E_004.eli: A lunchbox with a lid: heat can warm it, but the food cannot get out.
mem: Open: matter + energy
Closed: energy only
Isolated: neither
Isothermal = constant T, a process word
x5E_004.trap: Choosing isothermal because it sounds thermodynamic; it is not a boundary type.
x5E_004.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Elements in their standard state have ΔH°f = 0 by convention. Their entropy S° is still positive at 25 °C.
Correct. The third law says a perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K has only one possible arrangement (one microstate), so S = k ln 1 = 0.
Wrong. 0 °C is 273 K, not absolute zero, and gases have large positive entropy.
Wrong. A liquid at its freezing point is still disordered, with molecules moving, so entropy is well above zero.

p: Entropy (S) measures disorder, or how many ways particles can be arranged (microstates). At 0 K (absolute zero) all motion stops.
A perfect crystal at 0 K has just one arrangement, so entropy is exactly zero. Anything warmer or less ordered has positive entropy.

x5E_005.eli: A perfectly neat toy box where every toy has exactly one place: only one way to be tidy.
mem: S = 0 only for a perfect crystal at 0 K
Real substances above 0 K have S > 0
ΔH°f = 0 for elements in standard state (different idea)
S = k ln W, where W is number of microstates
x5E_005.trap: Mixing up the ΔH°f = 0 convention for elements with the entropy rule.
x5E_005.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Adiabatic means no heat flows (q = 0), so ΔU = w. The gas pushes outward and does work, so w is negative and U drops. For an ideal gas, lower U means lower T.
Wrong. No heat exchange does not mean constant T. Work alone can change internal energy. Constant T would be isothermal.
Wrong. More volume does not raise T here. Doing work costs the gas energy, so it cools.
Wrong. Heat capacity sets how big the drop is, not whether it goes up or down. The sign is set by ΔU = w < 0.

p: First law: ΔU = q + w, where U is internal energy, q is heat added to the gas, and w is work done on the gas. Adiabatic means q = 0.
When a gas expands it pushes on the surroundings, so it does work, and w is negative. With q = 0, U falls. For an ideal gas, U depends only on T, so T falls.

x5E_007.eli: A spray can feels cold because the gas spends its own energy pushing outward.
mem: Adiabatic: q = 0
Then ΔU = w
Expanding gas: w < 0, so T falls
Isothermal: T constant (ΔU = 0 for ideal gas)
x5E_007.sc: Adiabatic expansion cools, adiabatic compression heats.
x5E_007.trap: Equating 'no heat exchange' with 'no temperature change'.
x5E_007.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. A system's own entropy can fall, like water freezing, if the surroundings gain more entropy.
Wrong. Spontaneous processes can be endothermic (ΔH positive), such as ice melting at room temperature.
Correct. The second law says the entropy of the universe (system plus surroundings) increases in every spontaneous process.
Wrong. Energy of the universe is constant. That is the first law, not the second.

p: Entropy is a measure of disorder. The second law says total entropy of the universe, system plus surroundings, goes up in any spontaneous (natural) process.
One part can lose entropy if the other gains more. Water freezing in the cold lowers its own entropy but releases heat that raises the surroundings' entropy.

x5E_008.eli: Cleaning your room (less mess) takes work and makes a mess elsewhere. Overall, the mess in the world rises.
mem: Spontaneous: ΔS universe > 0
First law: energy of universe constant
System entropy alone does not decide spontaneity
x5E_008.trap: Applying the second law to the system alone instead of the universe.
x5E_008.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. A reversible process runs through equilibrium states and creates no new entropy. The system's change cancels the surroundings' change, so ΔS universe = 0.
Wrong. Positive ΔS universe describes real, irreversible spontaneous processes.
Wrong. A negative ΔS universe would break the second law.
Wrong. ΔH/T gives the system's entropy change for a reversible process at constant T and P, not the universe's.

p: A reversible process is an ideal, super-slow process that could be run backward with no leftover change. It stays at equilibrium the whole way.
Because nothing is lost to disorder, entropy gained by one part equals entropy lost by the other. The universe total is zero. Real processes are irreversible and have a positive total.

x5E_011.eli: Rolling a ball up and down a perfectly smooth hill with no friction: nothing is wasted.
mem: Reversible: ΔS universe = 0
Irreversible/spontaneous: ΔS universe > 0
Negative ΔS universe: impossible
x5E_011.trap: Confusing the system's ΔS (which can be nonzero) with the universe's ΔS.
x5E_011.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Many reactions are endothermic with positive ΔH. The sign has nothing to do with Hess's law.
Wrong. Heat at constant volume equals ΔU, not ΔH. It is not the basis of Hess's law.
Correct. Enthalpy is a state function: ΔH depends only on the start and end states, not on the path. So any series of steps adding up to the overall reaction gives the same total ΔH.
Wrong. ΔH is extensive and scales with the amount reacting. That is a true fact, but it is not why Hess's law works.

p: A state function depends only on where you start and finish, not how you got there. Enthalpy (H, heat content at constant pressure) is one.
Hess's law says you can add the ΔH of steps to get the ΔH of the overall reaction. This works because the path does not matter.

x5E_012.eli: Climbing from the bottom to the top of a hill, the height gained is the same no matter which trail you take.
mem: H is a state function
Hess: add ΔH of steps
Reverse a reaction: flip the sign of ΔH
Multiply a reaction: multiply ΔH
x5E_012.trap: Picking a true-sounding fact about ΔH that is not the reason Hess's law works.
x5E_012.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. This counts only one mole of water. The equation makes 2 H₂O, so multiply its ΔH°f by 2.
Wrong. This has the sign flipped, using reactants minus products. Always do products minus reactants.
Correct. ΔH° = [(-394) + 2(-286)] - [(-75)] = -966 + 75 = -891 kJ. O₂ is an element in its standard state, so its ΔH°f is 0.
Wrong. This adds the CH₄ value (-966 - 75) instead of subtracting it.

p: ΔH°f is the heat change when 1 mole of a compound forms from its elements in standard states. Elements themselves, like O₂, have ΔH°f = 0.
To find the reaction's ΔH°, add up the products (times their coefficients) and subtract the reactants (times theirs). Always products minus reactants.

x5E_015.eli: It is like your bank balance: what you end up with minus what you started with.
mem: ΔH°rxn = Σ n ΔH°f(products) - Σ n ΔH°f(reactants)
Elements in standard state: 0
Multiply by coefficients

fm.f: ΔH°rxn = Σ n ΔH°f(products) - Σ n ΔH°f(reactants), where n = coefficient, ΔH°f = formation enthalpy
fm.why: It uses formation enthalpies, which are tabulated, to get the reaction's heat.
fm.nc: 2 x 286 = 572, plus 394 = 966. Then subtract -75, which means add 75: 966 - 75 = 891.

x5E_015.sc: Combustion of a hydrocarbon is very exothermic, so expect a big negative answer.
x5E_015.trap: Forgetting to multiply by the coefficient, or reversing products minus reactants.
x5E_015.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Phase changes do not break covalent O-H bonds inside the molecule. They overcome attractions between molecules (intermolecular forces).
Wrong. ΔH of a phase change reflects how many attractions are overcome, not the temperature itself.
Wrong. It is ice that has the more complete, ordered hydrogen-bond network. Liquid water has some of those bonds broken or loosened already.
Correct. Vaporization separates molecules almost completely, overcoming nearly all hydrogen bonding. Melting only loosens part of the network so molecules can slide past each other.

p: Enthalpy of fusion is the heat needed to melt 1 mole of a solid. Enthalpy of vaporization is the heat needed to boil 1 mole of a liquid. Both fight intermolecular forces, here hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
In liquid water, molecules still stick to each other. In gas, they are far apart. So vaporization breaks far more attractions. For water, about 41 kJ/mol versus about 6 kJ/mol.

x5E_020.eli: Melting is like loosening a crowd's hands so people can move around. Vaporizing is sending every person to a different city.
mem: Phase changes break intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds
ΔHvap is much greater than ΔHfus
Water: about 41 vs 6 kJ/mol
x5E_020.trap: Thinking that boiling water breaks the O-H bonds inside each molecule.
x5E_020.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. The bond-energy method is built entirely on counting bonds broken and bonds formed. Trap: mixing up the method itself with its weakness.
Wrong. Bond energies are defined for molecules in the gas phase, not just liquids and solids. Trap: confusing which phase the values apply to.
Wrong. Bond enthalpies are heat (enthalpy) values only. Entropy is a separate quantity. Trap: thinking any energy table also holds entropy.
Correct. A table lists one average value for, say, C-H, taken over many molecules. The real C-H bond in a given molecule is a bit stronger or weaker, so the answer is only approximate.

p: Bond energy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in the gas phase. To estimate a reaction's enthalpy change, add up the energy of bonds broken and subtract the energy of bonds formed.

The tables list averages. A C-H bond is not identical in every molecule. Formation enthalpies (the heat to make one mole of a compound from its elements) are measured for each exact compound, so they are more accurate.

x5E_025.eli: Using bond energies is like guessing the price of every apple from the average apple price. Using formation values is like reading the real price tag on each apple.
mem: Bond energies are averages, so results are estimates
Breaking bonds costs energy (positive); forming bonds releases energy
Delta H(rxn) = bonds broken - bonds formed
Delta Hf values give exact answers through Hess's law

fm.f: Delta H(rxn) = sum of energies of bonds broken - sum of energies of bonds formed
fm.why: Shows why the method counts bonds, and why averaging adds error.

x5E_025.trap: Students pick an answer that sounds like a sloppy method. The real issue is only that tabulated values are averages.
x5E_025.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Melting absorbs heat and the liquid is more disordered, so Delta S is positive. Trap: a sign error.
Correct. At the melting point the change is reversible, so Delta S = q/T = 6000 J / 273 K, about +22 J/(mol K). Positive, because ice becomes a more disordered liquid.
Wrong. This is about 1000 times too small because 6.0 kJ was never converted to 6000 J. Trap: unit mismatch between kJ and J.
Wrong. The formula uses the constant temperature T, not a temperature change. Melting happens at a steady 0 C, and entropy is still well defined.

concept.t: Entropy change at a phase change
p: Entropy (S) measures disorder, or how spread out energy and particles are. When a substance changes phase at its melting point, heat goes in while the temperature stays fixed.
For a reversible change at constant temperature, Delta S = q/T, with T in kelvin. Here q equals the enthalpy of fusion, the heat needed to melt one mole.

x5E_033.eli: Melting is like a tidy stack of blocks being dumped onto the floor. The mess (entropy) goes up, and it takes heat to do it.
mem: Delta S = q(rev)/T, with T in kelvin
Melting and boiling have positive Delta S

p: Equilibrium shifts only when Q (the reaction quotient, computed like K but from current amounts) no longer equals K. Q depends on the concentrations or partial pressures of the reacting species.
